chapter: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
title: Ward Pinkett's death in 1937
summary: Pinkett, who had worked with Jelly Roll, died after a fall into a flooded basement while Caldwell was away on the road with Jesse Owens's band.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Well, what happened to him eventually? (Unintelligible)?

Yes, he did. Ward, we were living there when (unintelligible) I was with Tiny Bradshaw this guy named Reuben, and (unintelligible), but Jesse Owens -- who was he with -- we were with Jesse Owens, but Jesse Owens came back from the Olympics. He had taken Danny Logan's band, the trombone player, and then had a nice band. So Teddy Hill had a band up at Savoy. So most of the fellows in Danny's group, fellows that went to school, like I went to Wilberforce, lot of them went to this school; lot of them participated in athletics, track meet and all, and Jesse liked that.

So when Jesse came back from the Olympics, the looking agent said (unintelligible) all right, he wanted Danny's band because everybody liked what he liked, went to school, and that's what he wanted, and it was a good group. So we played around. I went over to see Ward, and we stopped in a little, old bar and grill. I see him before I go on this trip. We sat there and drank and talked. I said, I'll see you when I come back. I says, so I'll drop you a card. All the guys in the band knew him. Said, all right, Hap -- we sat there drinking -- said, you don't pay for anything.

So after we left, when we came back off the trip, the place where he was living (unintelligible) had flooded downstairs where we used to all go down and jam at this fellow's rooming house. Somehow or other, I guess he might have been a little tipsy and fell down them stairs and, I guess -- and water, you know,

Water -- he fell down there in that old water, you know, in that -- seeped, you know, the basement had flooded. That's the story he gave me, because I imagine when he fell he struck his head or something, see.
Yeah. When we came -- when we got back, they had sent his body back to Newport News, Virginia. for burial (Unintelligible) that's his home, Newport News, Virginia.
Well, I mean was he sort of drinking a lot in --

Well, we'd drink. He wasn't what you'd call a sloppy drinker. He was just -- drink a casual drink, like (unintelligible) if at night when I say I wanted to see him before we pull out that morning, and I go and see my buddy over there and we have a few drinks. He lived just across the street from the bar and grill, and we'd sit there and talk, talk about an hour and a half, few drinks. Said, well, Ward, I'll catch you when I come back.
Well, he -- I mean what I was wondering, you know, he made the records with Jelly Roll, but then you don't hear much of him lately.
Well, he got on -- he got in some kind of -- well, he was in love with -- she was -- used to be
up to the Savoy. She was a hostess. I think he was too much wrapped up in her. Then when he started to drinking, he didn't become a liquor hound, but he was enough to --
That's right. That's when we left for this conference with Jesse Owens, 1937. That's right.

Yeah. Well, you see, I mean he was with Rex Church band in '33, with Teddy Hill's at the Lafayette in '34, and during 1935 worked with Albert Rollini at Adrian Top Room Lew's also played briefly with Louis Louie, died of pheumonia.

That's right. Well, a cold, (unintelligible) when he caught that, got wet down there, and then he wasn't never no big fellow, but he was, weighed about 100 and, say, 55 pounds. He wasn't no big, husky fellow, you know. Very good trumpet player.
